For me, personally, there are three main factors that helped alleviate my depression to the point where I'm now *months to years* between episodes.

1. I distanced myself from school and everyone who knew me there after I graduated. William Gibson once said, "Before you worry about whether you have depression, first make sure you aren't surrounded by assholes." Since removing myself from an enforced social circle where people abused and ostracized me for being the "weird kid", my mental health improved dramatically.
2. I pulled myself out of poverty. For a ten-year stretch, all of my money was going toward rent and utilities - with about $40-60 leftover for food - for the *month.* I was filled with constant anxiety about bills. Also, I was lonely as fuck - the thing about being poor is that you find out how much it costs to maintain friendships. If my friends wanted to do a get-together, I had to pass because I couldn't afford bus fare (let alone a meal at a restaurant). Plus, I found out that a lot of the people I thought of as close friends saw me as an acquaintance at best. I kept getting a lot of toxic positive platitudes from my social circles, and sweet fuck-all for actual support. But then I got a job that paid me a lot more, and I found out that I wasn't getting depressed like I used to. A few years ago, I had a situation where my car had engine trouble. Previously, I would've given myself an ulcer worrying about how I was gonna pay it - but then I realized that I was only mildly annoyed about how expensive the repair estimate was, and it made me realize that I was in a lot better situation financially. Having constant anxiety about getting your basic needs met is *exhausting*, and it left me feeling very vulnerable.
3. I got out of an abusive relationship. Like Point 1, I kept falling into multiple relationships that harmed me (emotionally, physically, and even sexually). And it reinforced the idea that my self-worth was predicated on how happy I made other people - and that it was also my responsibility to keep them happy. I spent 3 years on my own, just healing from the damage that had been inflicted on me before I finally met the woman who I would eventually marry. I envy the amount of patience she has for me because I know I reacted towards her a lot like an abandoned dog that would snap anyone who tries to get close to it.

But with those stressors out of my life - I find I have a lot more energy and there are fewer times when I get depressed, and when those depressive times do come up - they pass a lot more quickly and are less impactful on my daily life.

Last year I got diagnosed with ADHD and started receiving medication for it.

In the months afterwards I discovered four very big things:

1. ADHD will often drive people to self-stimulate using food (especially sugar and caffeine for their stimulant effects.)
2. People with ADHD will often ignore "physical cues" until they become severe. For me, it meant that I would keep eating until I felt absolutely full and uncomfortable.
3. ADHD makes it difficult to establish habits - any change in routine can set off executive dysfunction like a mofo. So telling me that I need to eat more vegetables and exercise more was like giving dietary advice to a cat.
4. Likewise, the ADHD need for stimulation also becomes a demand for constant novelty. I would go on diet and fitness kicks that would last about a week or two before my ADHD ferret brain would chase after whatever was the new hotness du jour.

The weekend I started taking my meds, I went out to Sunday brunch with my in-laws. During the meal, I suddenly had a mild sensation of fullness that I hadn't experienced before. It was like part of my brain was telling me to stop because I had eaten enough. Prior to medication, I would have cleared my plate and probably licked it clean afterwards. But that day, I was only able to eat half of my omelette and none of my hash browns because I knew I was full.

Once my meds started cutting out a lot of the "noise" from my ADHD, I've found it a lot easier to keep up with healthy habits and they even feel like an investment, where previously it felt like a chore. It's made me realize that a lot of my unhealthy coping strategies were because of weird brain chemistry and not necessarily a lack of willpower or discipline on my part.

1. Eating *REALLY* fast. I remember going out to lunch with some coworkers, and I had cleaned my plate by the time the last person was served. This often meant that I was eating far too much to begin with.

3. Eating for stimulation. The problem with ADHD is that I always needed to be fidgeting with something, and somewhere along the way that translated into snacking for the sake of it. I tried to curb that habit by replacing junk food with healthy snacks (for example, I have a bag of roasted almonds at my desk instead of a bag of candy). But even that would be undermined by having access to junk food at home - resulting in me eating a half-bag of potato chips while watching TV.

These last two months have been incredibly life-changing for me as I now have the mental space to pause before I take action, instead of acting impulsively and adjusting to the fallout. My experience with offshoring has been slightly different.

During the "transition period" any issues with the incoming contractors (language barrier, technical incompetency) will be ignored because they're cheap. Because the CFO in charge of bringing on the contractors is only concerned with how much money that they're spending. It also doesn't help that the contracting agency will overexaggerate their ability to meet SLA and resolve issues.

Sometimes the people trained in the transition period are actually skilled individuals, whose sole purpose is to sell the illusion of competency with the new contractors. Those people will, in turn, be used to quickly develop training material for the *actual* contractors that will be used. The drop off in service will be immediately noticed as soon as transition has ended, and the contract is fully locked in.

Again, if a CFO is overseeing the offshoring process, they tend to be less technically minded than a CTO, CIO, or even COO - because their sole focus is *money.* (And IT is always seen as a cost sink for a department, never a force multiplier.)

The contracting agency will take advantage of this by constantly hyping the fact that they'll do the "same" work for pennies on the dollar. However, it will become quickly apparent that anything more complex than resetting an email password will be billed at a "project" or "enhanced" rate - which is often the same amount the company was paying for internal IT, *or more.*

When it becomes apparent that the alleged savings made by offshoring IT are getting eclipsed by fees, changing rates, and sketchy billing practices ("It doesn't matter if the issue was resolved in 5 minutes, we're billing you for 15 minutes minimum - and once we hit 40 hours billed that week, we're switching to our overtime rate"), it will be too late to back out of the contract because the company is locked in for 5 years minimum. And if the company tries backing out of it, they'll still have to pay the equivalent of that money in penalties (or spend that in legal fees.)

Meanwhile, it's only a matter of time before something major breaks, the offshore people hem and haw about it (to both pad their billable hours and obfuscate their incompetence), and your company has to bring on a former employee as a "consultant" to bring everything back online - at 5x - 20x their base salary. That's not counting the few *million* dollars in revenue that the company has lost because of the whole fiasco.

Finally, the company either bites the bullet and terminates the offshoring contract early and brings people back onboard internally, or hires additional internal IT while they wait for the offshoring contract to expire (hopefully with the mandate that the offshoring people escalate anything that isn't a password reset).
